plot_extraction.response_text:
Publishers Sloper and Dodge face ruin when Australians violently drive away their book canvassers, leaving the firm unable to sell a costly new atlas. An inventor offers them a mechanical, cast-iron canvasser that can deliver an enormous sales pitch, withstand dogs and beatings, retaliate with a devastating punch, and automatically collect signed orders.

They test the automaton in the lethargic town of Ninemile, first sending it to Macpherson, a huge land agent who despises canvassers. Macpherson’s dog bites off part of its tar-padded leg, and when Macpherson strikes it, the machine knocks him unconscious. Its handlers flee when a police sergeant, O’Grady, arrives.

Mistaking the machine first for a drunk and then recognizing it as a canvasser, O’Grady tries to lead it to jail. His touch activates its arm, which traps him in a crushing embrace while it marches toward the river, endlessly shouting its sales pitch. Constable Dooley attempts a rescue but is knocked senseless by the machine. Still clutching the terrified sergeant, the automaton falls into Ninemile Creek, drowning them both.

The incident is never properly reported and fades into local legend. The inventor later drinks himself to death, while Dooley advances in the police, Sloper becomes a minister, and Dodge enters Parliament.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a fast-moving comic bush yarn shaped by broad satire, escalating farce and deadpan exaggeration. Its narrator is omniscient, confident and conversational, recounting absurd events with the composure of a factual report. This contrast between sober delivery and grotesque incident is central to the humour: canvassers are tarred, feathered, harrowed and threatened with abandoned mine shafts, while the narration treats such violence as an ordinary commercial difficulty. Occasional direct addresses to “the reader” strengthen the manner of an oral storyteller who assumes a knowing, socially familiar audience.

The tone is irreverent, exuberant and mock-serious. Hyperbole appears almost continuously: smoke can cause paralysis, mosquitoes fall asleep before biting, genealogies stretch back to Noah’s Ark, and punches propel victims figuratively into the following week. Violent action is rendered as slapstick rather than tragedy, with bodies knocked down, dragged away or drowned in sequences governed by comic machinery. Institutions and respectable roles receive the same treatment as individuals. Publishers are predatory, inventors unreliable, police cowardly or incompetent, politicians absurdly rewarded, and religious respectability becomes part of the final joke. The satire is therefore genial in manner but broadly cynical in outlook.

The diction combines formal narrative phrasing with Australian colonial slang, commercial jargon, sporting language and colloquial idiom. Elevated expressions such as “divers strange bush ways,” “durance vile” and “superlative Dutch courage” sit beside “big bug,” “yabber,” “bloke,” “clout” and “gone in the horrors.” This mixing of registers creates comic incongruity and gives the prose a distinctly late-colonial Australian character. Period references to boxing, political agitation, temperance, book canvassing and remote settlements establish the social world without lengthy exposition.

Dialogue is highly characterising and often dialectal. Dodge’s brisk American manner, the inventor’s enthusiastic patter and O’Grady’s phonetic Irish speech distinguish speakers immediately. The canvasser’s prerecorded sales pitch parodies inflated advertising language: its impossible premiums, extravagant claims and relentless verbosity transform commercial persuasion into an assault. Repetition is especially effective when this sales spiel continues unchanged through fights and arrests, making the automaton’s verbal persistence as threatening as its mechanical strength. The phonetic rendering of accents is broad and caricatural, reflecting the comic conventions and ethnic stereotypes of the period.

Sentences vary between expansive descriptive passages and short action beats. Long cumulative sentences pile up details, examples and increasingly implausible qualifications, while abrupt declarations—“It was a fatal mistake”—signal a new stage in the disaster. Parenthetical comments, dashes, lists and semicolons help preserve the rhythm of spoken anecdote. Similes are vivid, physical and deliberately excessive: smoke behaves like a locomotive, a struck man drops “like a fowl,” and a mechanical blow arrives with the force of a horse-kick. Descriptions favour memorable grotesque particulars over realism, as in Macpherson’s enormous freckles and horn-like moustache.

Characterisation is economical and caricatural. Each person is built around a few enlarged traits: Sloper is bald and sanctimonious, Dodge small and smoky, Macpherson gigantic and combative, O’Grady persuasive but conflict-averse, and Dooley immensely strong yet sleepy and cowardly when defeated. Names and nicknames—Sloper, Dodge, the Genius, the Wombat—have a comic emblematic quality. Psychological depth is secondary to function within the farce; characters exist largely to trigger, misunderstand or suffer from the automaton’s mechanisms.

The structure follows a clear pattern of setup, demonstration, field test and runaway catastrophe. The opening establishes the hostility toward canvassers and the publishers’ financial crisis; the invention then appears as an apparently perfect solution. Ninemile provides a contained comic arena in which each encounter raises the stakes: hostile land agent, dog, sergeant, constable and finally the river. Much of the plotting depends on mechanical cause and effect, with every touch activating another spring and every attempted intervention worsening the situation. The ending compresses the aftermath into a mock-chronicle of deaths, promotions and political success, then reduces the extraordinary adventure to a garbled local legend. This deflation supplies the final ironic stroke.

The setting is presented through comic regionalism. The bush town’s heat, lethargy, whisky culture, local rivalries and indifference to outside authority are exaggerated into a self-contained social mythology. Ninemile is so apathetic that even a spectacular death fails to reach the newspapers, while a campaign to secure the Federal Capital instantly displaces all concern. The result is a style that blends tall tale, colonial sketch, technological fantasy and institutional satire. Its signature qualities are narrative briskness, vernacular energy, grotesque hyperbole, mechanical escalation, mock-documentary authority and a cheerful willingness to turn commercial modernity and civic respectability into anarchic farce.

## THE IRON CANVASSER

The publishing firm of Sloper and Dodge had made its reputation by selling books which nobody wished to read to persons who could not afford to buy them. This is the foundation of the publishing trade, and explains why Mr. Sloper occupied a large office furnished in red morocco while many of his customers slept on flour-bags.

Sloper was a broad, bald man with a sanctimonious chin and a watch-chain like a ship’s cable. Dodge, his partner, was small, sharp, American, and so continuously surrounded by cigar-smoke that clerks entering his room frequently suffered temporary paralysis. Between them they had issued *The Imperial, Universal, Historical, Geographical, Geological and Domestic Atlas of the Civilised and Uncivilised World*, in six volumes, with an index, a supplement, and portraits of eminent subscribers.

The work was magnificent. It contained maps of countries that no longer existed, coloured pictures of fishes that never had existed, and statistics prepared with such care that every total disagreed with every other total on the same page. The retail price was twelve guineas, payable in weekly instalments extending far beyond the probable life of the purchaser. With each set went a presentation engraving of Her Majesty, a family medicine chest, a certificate of intellectual distinction, and, for immediate orders, a patent corkscrew.

Unfortunately, the Australian public declined to purchase it.

Sloper and Dodge employed twenty-seven canvassers to carry the gospel of the Atlas through the continent. Of these, three returned within a month. One had been tarred and feathered near Wagga; one had been attached to a stump-jump plough and harrowed across forty acres of light loam; and one had escaped from a deserted mine shaft by climbing a rope composed of his own order forms. The remaining twenty-four were variously missing, married, converted to honest labour, or lying low under assumed names.

The reports that reached the firm were discouraging.

“Dear Sirs,” wrote a canvasser from the Darling, “I regret I cannot continue in your service, having been bitten by the local vigilance committee.”

Another stated that the inhabitants of an inland township had listened patiently to the full description of the work and then escorted him seventeen miles into the bush without horse, boots, compass, or trousers.

A third had induced a selector to sign an order, but the selector subsequently discovered that the signature was binding. He pursued the canvasser with a shovel, recovered the order, and inserted it, together with portions of the canvasser’s coat, into the hollow of a burning tree.

“It is prejudice,” said Sloper.

“It is assault and battery,” said Dodge. “And it’s cutting into profits.”

They sat opposite one another in the office, separated by an account-book showing that forty thousand copies of the Atlas had been printed and eleven sold. Of the eleven, four had been returned, two had been exchanged for groceries, and one subscriber was suing the firm on the ground that the map of Queensland had frightened his children.

“We require,” said Sloper, “a canvasser of courage, endurance, address, persuasive eloquence, and Christian fortitude.”

“What we require,” said Dodge, “is a canvasser they can’t kill.”

At that instant the door opened and a little man entered carrying a black bag.

He had long hair, bright eyes, an alpaca coat, and the expression of one who has just invented perpetual motion and requires five shillings to complete it. He bowed, struck his bag against the doorpost, apologised to the bag, and placed a soiled card before the partners.

It bore the words:

**PROFESSOR SEPTIMUS WOMBATT**  
**Mechanical Genius, Electro-Phrenologist, Inventor**  
**Confidential Experiments Undertaken**

“I have solved your difficulty,” he said.

Dodge looked at him through the smoke.

“Which difficulty? We’ve got a selection.”

“The hostility of the public toward the travelling representative.”

Sloper folded his hands upon his waistcoat.

“You propose to soften the public?”

“No, sir. I propose to harden the representative.”

The Genius opened his bag and produced springs, brass wheels, a small hammer, several screws, and a sketch of an iron man. He spread the sketch on the table and tapped it with an enthusiastic forefinger.

“My Patent Automatic Commercial Advocate,” he said, “combines eloquence with invulnerability. It can traverse eighty miles per day, deliver a persuasive address of four hours and thirteen minutes without repetition—except where repetition is commercially desirable—resist dogs, stones, sticks, boiling water and ordinary firearms, secure the subscriber’s signature, detach the order, place it in a locked receptacle, and continue to the next residence.”

“Can it take a punch?” asked Dodge.

The Genius smiled pityingly.

“The frame is cast iron; the exterior is sheet steel; the joints are manganese bronze; and the trousers are padded with tarred rope. A man striking it would experience sensations comparable to kicking a municipal bridge.”

“Can it give a punch?”

The Genius became solemn.

“In self-defence only. Pressure upon the left breast-plate releases an eight-horse spiral spring operating the right arm. The return blow has been calculated at one ton, three hundredweight, less friction.”

Sloper glanced toward the door, as if expecting a procession of ruined debtors.

“Would that be legal?”

“Perfectly,” said the Genius. “The machine has no criminal intention.”

Within a week the partners visited an abandoned coach factory at the edge of the city, where Professor Wombatt had constructed the Automatic Commercial Advocate. It stood seven feet high and weighed nearly half a ton. Its head was painted pink, its eyes were blue glass, and its black iron moustache curved upward with a confidence rarely met outside patent medicine advertisements. It wore a frock-coat of boiler plate, steel boots, and a bell-shaped hat riveted to the skull.

Across its chest appeared the words:

**SLOPER & DODGE—KNOWLEDGE BROUGHT TO THE HOME**

A speaking trumpet occupied the place ordinarily assigned to the mouth. In its right hand it carried a specimen volume; in its left, an order-book and self-inking pen.

The Genius wound the machine with a windlass and pressed a stud behind its ear.

The iron eyes rolled. The chest clicked. One foot advanced.

“GOOD MORNING, SIR OR MADAM,” it proclaimed in a voice capable of addressing a public meeting during artillery practice. “HAVE YOU CONSIDERED THE MORAL, SOCIAL, COMMERCIAL AND MATRIMONIAL ADVANTAGES OF ACCURATE GEOGRAPHICAL INFORMATION?”

The windows shook.

“Reduce it,” said Sloper.

Professor Wombatt adjusted a screw.

The machine continued in a confidential roar.

“THIS UNRIVALLED WORK, PREPARED BY NINETY-SEVEN DISTINGUISHED SCHOLARS, NINE EXPLORERS, THREE BISHOPS AND A PRACTICAL TAXIDERMIST, PLACES THE ENTIRE GLOBE WITHIN REACH OF THE HUMBLEST HOME.”

It extended the order-book. Dodge took the pen experimentally. The iron fingers closed upon his wrist and guided his hand toward the dotted line.

“Here!” he cried.

“The collecting gear,” explained the Genius. “It assumes reluctance to be muscular hesitation and assists the subscriber.”

Dodge signed. The machine released him, tore out the order, posted it through a slot in its own ribs, and resumed:

“TO THE FIRST FIVE THOUSAND SUBSCRIBERS WE PRESENT, WITHOUT EXTRA CHARGE, A MAGNIFICENT STEEL ENGRAVING OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE, A HOUSEHOLD GUIDE TO ETIQUETTE, AND A COMPLETE SET OF FALSE TEETH, SIZES TO BE SELECTED AFTER DELIVERY.”

Sloper’s eyes shone.

“It is Providence,” he said.

“It is business,” said Dodge. “Where do we try it?”

Now, the prudent man tests a new gun where there is nobody to shoot, and the experienced publisher tests a canvasser where the population is too scattered to combine against him. They selected Ninemile.

Ninemile lay beside a brown creek in a fold of the western plains. It possessed a hotel, a police station, a store, a blacksmith’s shed and thirty-one inhabitants, counting a Chinese gardener who denied responsibility for the census. The town was named Ninemile because it stood eleven miles from everywhere. In summer the heat melted candles inside locked cupboards; in winter the wind removed roofs and distributed them among the neighbouring districts.

The inhabitants were celebrated for their repose. The publican’s clock had stopped in 1889, and nobody had yet found the energy to wind it. Smoke from the chimneys rose ten feet, reconsidered the matter, and lay down. Mosquitoes approaching the town fell asleep before biting and had to be carried home by relatives.

In this favourable market resided Angus Macpherson, land agent, commission broker, auctioneer, breeder of dogs and enemy of canvassers.

Macpherson stood six feet seven in his socks, though no man had ever seen him in his socks and lived to measure him. His hands resembled uncooked hams; his freckles were as large as half-crowns; and his red moustache projected on either side of his face like the horns of an irritated bullock. His ancestry, according to himself, went back through Robert Bruce, Julius Caesar and a second cousin of Noah who missed the Ark through a misunderstanding about the sailing date.

Macpherson had once purchased a twelve-volume history from a canvasser. On discovering that the last eight volumes consisted mainly of footnotes to the first four, he swore an oath extending from sunset until breakfast. Since then he had received commercial travellers with a stockwhip.

“He is the severe test,” said Sloper.

“He is the sale we need,” said Dodge.

Professor Wombatt and the two publishers arrived at Ninemile by goods train with the machine packed in a crate labelled AGRICULTURAL IMPLEMENT—THIS SIDE UP. It had travelled from the city upside down, but iron constitutions are less sensitive to railway management than human ones.

They lodged at the hotel under fictitious names. Next morning, before the population had begun considering whether to get out of bed, they wheeled the Advocate to the road leading to Macpherson’s house.

The Genius wound it, pointed it at the gate and pressed the stud.

“GOOD MORNING, SIR OR MADAM,” bellowed the machine, and set off at a steady march.

The three experimenters followed at a prudent distance behind a row of pepper trees.

Macpherson’s dog was named Presbyterian because it distrusted strangers and believed firmly in punishment. It was a brindled brute with the chest of a bull, the jaws of a rabbit trap and the private habits of a crocodile. Hearing the Advocate, it came through the fence without troubling the gate and seized the machine by the calf.

There was a noise like a saw entering hardwood.

Presbyterian bit through the steel cloth, removed six inches of tarred rope padding, and retired with its mouth stuck together. It rolled upon the ground, sneezed, and looked at the machine with astonished reproach.

The Advocate did not vary its pace.

“WITHIN THESE SUMPTUOUSLY ILLUSTRATED PAGES,” it announced, “THE READER MAY VISIT THE SNOWS OF THE ARCTIC, THE JUNGLES OF AFRICA AND THE PRINCIPAL RAILWAY REFRESHMENT ROOMS OF AUSTRALASIA WITHOUT LEAVING THE DOMESTIC FIRESIDE.”

Macpherson appeared on the veranda in shirt-sleeves.

“Clear out!” he said.

“THE CLIMATE OF PATAGONIA—”

“Clear out, ye boiler-plated nuisance!”

“—IS FULLY DESCRIBED, TOGETHER WITH THE HABITS OF THE LLAMA, THE CUSTOMS OF THE NATIVES, AND RELIABLE INSTRUCTIONS FOR REMOVING INK FROM CARPETS.”

Macpherson descended the steps. The earth moved slightly under him. He walked round the machine, observed the order-book, and understood its profession.

“A canvasser,” he whispered.

There are moments when an old wrong rises before a man with terrible clearness. Macpherson remembered the twelve-volume history, the instalments, and the footnotes. With a roar he struck the Advocate upon the left breast-plate.

It was a fatal mistake.

A spring snapped inside the machine. The right arm vanished and reappeared. There was a sound resembling a horse kicking an empty tank, and Macpherson travelled backward through the veranda rail, across a cane chair, and into a rainwater barrel. The barrel burst. Macpherson emerged briefly amid hoops and water, looked surprised, and fell like a fowl shot during an argument.

The Advocate extended its order-book toward him.

“THE PRICE OF THIS IMPERISHABLE MONUMENT OF HUMAN LEARNING IS LESS THAN THE WEEKLY EXPENDITURE OF THE AVERAGE FAMILY UPON PICKLES.”

Behind the pepper trees, Sloper removed his hat.

“Powerful,” he said.

“Too powerful,” said Dodge.

Professor Wombatt was pale.

“The spring requires moderation.”

Presbyterian, having freed its jaws by swallowing most of the padding, crawled beneath the house and abandoned public life. The three men hurried toward the machine, intending to switch it off. Then Sergeant O’Grady appeared at the gate.

O’Grady was a round, persuasive policeman whose courage was chiefly conversational. He could pacify two fighting men by explaining that Constable Dooley was coming, and could pacify Dooley by explaining that the fighting men had gone. Through these arrangements he had preserved the King’s peace for fourteen years without doing anything calculated to disturb his own.

He surveyed the wrecked veranda, the unconscious Macpherson, and the iron stranger.

“What’s this, now?”

The Advocate marched toward the road.

“GOOD MORNING, SIR OR MADAM.”

“Drunk,” said O’Grady. “And disorderly.”

Sloper, Dodge and the Genius silently withdrew behind a haystack.

O’Grady approached the machine with official majesty.

“Come along quiet, me fine fellow. There’s no use makin’ a noise about it.”

“DO YOU KNOW THAT THE AMAZON RIVER DISCHARGES A VOLUME OF WATER SUFFICIENT TO SUPPLY EVERY HOUSEHOLD IN THE EMPIRE WITH THREE BATHS DAILY?”

“Canvasser!” said O’Grady, stepping back.

He had faced drunken shearers, runaway horses and a deputation of ratepayers, but the travelling book agent touched an older fear. Still, Macpherson lay among the ruins, and the law must occasionally be seen from the hotel veranda to be doing something.

“In the King’s name,” said O’Grady, “I arrest ye for assault, drunkenness, damage to property, and speakin’ without reasonable excuse.”

He took hold of the Advocate’s left arm.

The Genius, watching from the haystack, made a small choking sound.

“What?” whispered Dodge.

“That operates the subscription grip.”

The iron arm swung outward, circled O’Grady’s waist and drew him against the machine’s ribs. His helmet fell over one eye. His toes barely touched the ground.

“Release me!” he gasped.

The Advocate marched on.

“NO HOME IS COMPLETE WITHOUT THIS TREASURY OF KNOWLEDGE. NO PARENT CAN NEGLECT IT WITHOUT IMPERILLING THE FUTURE OF THE CHILD.”

“Ow! Murder! Put me down, ye iron lunatic!”

O’Grady struggled, thereby increasing the pressure. The arm tightened until his uniform buttons left the force in several directions. One struck the hotel sign; another broke a window; a third was afterward found embedded in a pumpkin.

The machine turned toward the creek.

“Sign the order!” cried Professor Wombatt from concealment. “It may release you!”

“What order?”

“The Atlas!”

“I’ll buy it! I’ll buy two! Take the whole of me pay!”

But the order-book was in the Advocate’s other hand, beyond O’Grady’s reach. The machine’s internal pen waved cheerfully.

By this time Ninemile had awakened. Men emerged from the hotel carrying glasses they had not had time to put down. Women leaned over fences. Children followed at a distance, throwing stones until informed that the object was a canvasser, whereupon they found heavier stones.

Constable Dooley was asleep in the police station.

Dooley weighed seventeen stone and possessed shoulders broad enough to advertise on. In his youth he had thrown a professional wrestler through the wall of a tent; in middle age he preferred not to revive the habit, as violence made him thirsty and the Government allowance did not cover consequences. His courage was sound when fully awake, but he required forty minutes to attain that condition.

A boy rushed in shouting that Sergeant O’Grady had been captured by a talking boiler and was proceeding toward the river.

Dooley opened one eye.

“Tell him I’m busy.”

“It’s squeezin’ him to death.”

“Tell it to stop.”

“It won’t.”

Dooley sat up, buckled on his belt, put his boots upon the wrong feet, corrected the error, and came into the street carrying a baton.

The Advocate approached with O’Grady pinned to its side.

“THIS SUPERB ATLAS CONTAINS FOUR HUNDRED MAPS, EIGHT HUNDRED PLATES, NINE THOUSAND ENGRAVINGS, AND A COLOURED DIAGRAM EXPLAINING THE BRITISH CONSTITUTION TO THOSE WHO HAVE NEVER SEEN ONE.”

“Dooley!” shrieked O’Grady. “Save me!”

Dooley planted himself in the road.

“Release that officer.”

“THE MAPS ARE PRINTED IN COLOURS OF UNEXAMPLED BRILLIANCE—”

“Release him, or I’ll use force.”

“Use diplomacy!” cried O’Grady. “Force is what started it!”

Dooley struck the machine’s arm with his baton. The baton broke. Half flew into the store; the other half remained in his hand and gave him the appearance of a man threatening a locomotive with a clothes-peg.

The Advocate kept marching.

Dooley seized it around the waist. His muscles rose like sacks beneath his tunic. For one glorious second the machine stopped. The townspeople cheered. Dooley heaved; the road cracked under his boots; perspiration issued from him in quantities sufficient for irrigation.

Then his hand slipped upward and pressed the left breast-plate.

It was the same fatal mistake, at a more public moment.

The right arm delivered its commercial rejoinder. Dooley rose from the road, described a curve of uncommon scientific interest, passed through a stack of empty kerosene tins and came to rest beneath the blacksmith’s horse trough. The horse looked in, decided against drinking, and went away.

“Good man, Dooley,” murmured O’Grady. “Try again when ye wake up.”

Nobody else offered assistance. Ninemile courage was not deficient, but it was selective. The blacksmith proposed shooting the machine, until the storekeeper reminded him that the sergeant was attached. The publican suggested a rope, then recollected that his rope had been lent to the Progress Association in 1894. Macpherson, recovering sufficiently to crawl to the gate, shouted advice which was impressive in tone but unfit for mechanical application.

Behind the haystack the publishers held a conference.

“Switch it off,” said Sloper.

“We must reach the stud,” said the Genius.

“You invented it,” said Dodge. “Reach.”

“My life belongs to science.”

“Our money belongs to that machine.”

The Advocate came to the slope above Ninemile Creek. The creek was neither wide nor handsome, but a recent storm upstream had filled it with twelve feet of muddy water, drowned timber and objects which no respectable stream would admit carrying.

O’Grady saw the river.

“Turn round!” he cried. “Station’s the other way!”

“THE WORK IS STRONGLY BOUND IN MOROCCO-GRAINED CLOTH, RESISTANT TO DUST, MILDEW, CHILDREN, TERMITES AND ORDINARY DOMESTIC UNHAPPINESS.”

The iron feet entered the mud.

Professor Wombatt ran from concealment at last.

“Stop!” he shouted. “You’re exceeding the demonstration!”

The machine descended the bank. O’Grady clutched its neck, its hat and finally its speaking trumpet.

“Holy saints,” he said, “I’ll sign anything!”

“THE FIRST PAYMENT OF FIVE SHILLINGS SECURES IMMEDIATE DELIVERY.”

Water reached its knees.

Sloper and Dodge arrived at the top of the bank, but commercial instinct restrained them from going farther. The Genius slid halfway down, grasped a bush and called technical directions which the machine disregarded.

“Pull the lever beneath the right shoulder!”

“I can’t reach it!”

“Press the red stud!”

“They’re all mud-coloured!”

Water reached the Advocate’s waist. O’Grady’s helmet floated away. The current took his boots next, which was remarkable, as they had been issued two sizes too small.

“Tell me wife,” he called, “that I died on duty!”

“You’re not married,” shouted Dooley faintly from beneath the trough.

“Then tell nobody!”

The machine marched into the deepest channel.

“AS A FINAL INDUCEMENT, EACH SUBSCRIBER RECEIVES ABSOLUTELY FREE A HANDSOME CERTIFICATE SUITABLE FOR FRAMING—”

Its iron hat disappeared. For several seconds the speaking trumpet continued beneath the water, producing bubbles of salesmanship. The bubbles moved downstream, still numerous and persuasive, and then ceased.

Sergeant O’Grady and the Automatic Commercial Advocate were seen no more.

There was some talk of recovering them. Dooley declined to dive on medical grounds. Macpherson declared the creek bottom Crown land under agency to himself and demanded a search fee. The publican organised a rescue committee, which met in the bar and remained there until its funds were exhausted.

Sloper, Dodge and Professor Wombatt left Ninemile that night on a hand trolley. They took the order box with them, the machine having ejected it automatically before entering the creek. It contained Macpherson’s involuntary mark, O’Grady’s fingerprints, and an order signed by Dodge during the factory demonstration. The firm delivered all three sets of the Atlas and pursued payment with its customary devotion to principle.

No complete report of the disaster reached the newspapers. Dooley prepared one, but fell asleep over the second page. The first page merely stated that the sergeant was absent from duty under circumstances requiring explanation, and the Department returned it for additional particulars. Before these could be supplied, Ninemile began a campaign to become the Federal Capital. Public attention was diverted, and O’Grady’s disappearance passed into municipal tradition.

For years afterward children were warned not to swim in the creek, because an iron man lived at the bottom and would sell them six volumes of geography. During floods, settlers sometimes heard a hollow voice beneath the bridge discoursing upon the mineral resources of Bolivia; but sensible persons attributed this to frogs, whisky, or politics.

Professor Wombatt attempted to construct a mechanical temperance lecturer, but made the unhappy mistake of testing it in a public house. The machine was destroyed, and the Genius, finding science ungrateful, took to drink. He died some years later while explaining to a lamp-post an invention for converting seawater into brandy.

Constable Dooley was promoted for conspicuous gallantry in attempting the rescue. He ultimately became an inspector and was respected throughout the service as a man who never rushed into danger until it had been officially reported over.

Sloper abandoned publishing, entered the ministry, and acquired a reputation for sermons of extraordinary length. Those who heard him preach declared that his gestures occasionally resembled the action of a powerful spiral spring.

Dodge entered Parliament, where his experience with automatic speech proved invaluable. He became a Minister, survived three scandals, and was eventually knighted for services which nobody could precisely remember.

As for the Atlas, it sold out within ten years. Every police station in the colony was supplied with a set, the Government having decided that accurate geographical knowledge was essential to the preservation of public order.

Ninemile received two copies.

One was used to raise the sergeant’s desk to a comfortable height.

The other was placed in the local museum, beside O’Grady’s recovered helmet, under a card stating that he had been drowned while heroically saving an unknown traveller from the creek.

Thus history is made accurate, provided it is strongly bound, handsomely illustrated, and sold to the public by persons whom the public cannot conveniently knock down.

# The Cartographer of Lost Roads

Every morning, before the town awakened, Elias Vale walked to the eastern gate and drew a road that no longer existed.

He worked in chalk on the broad black stones beneath the arch. First came two parallel lines, pale and uncertain in the dawn. Then he added the milestones, the ash trees, the wooden bridge over the River Orr, and, beyond the bridge, the long curve where the road disappeared into the hills.

By sunrise, carts and boots had smudged the drawing. By noon, it was gone.

The people of Bellweather had learned not to ask why he continued.

Elias had once been the kingdom’s finest cartographer. His maps hung in council chambers and ship cabins, in schools and roadside inns. Travelers trusted the small precision of his hand: the exact bend of a stream, the warning mark for unstable cliffs, the tiny stars indicating places where water could be found in dry seasons.

He had mapped every road in the northern province except one.

The Old East Road had vanished seventeen years ago.

It had not fallen into ruin or been swallowed by forest. It had disappeared in a single night. One evening, merchants returned along it with wagons full of salt and blue glass. The next morning, the eastern gate opened onto a field of silver grass stretching unbroken to the horizon.

Search parties found no wheel tracks, no bridge, no hills, no trace of the villages that had stood along the route. Even the River Orr had altered its course. The world beyond the gate seemed to have folded itself shut.

Most people eventually accepted the loss. Elias did not.

His wife, Mara, had been traveling on the Old East Road that night.

For seventeen years, he had drawn it from memory.

One autumn morning, as Elias knelt beneath the eastern arch, a young girl stopped beside him. She wore an oversized green coat, and her dark hair had been cut unevenly, as if with a kitchen knife.

“You have the bridge wrong,” she said.

Elias looked up.

No one criticized his maps.

“The bridge had six posts,” the girl continued. “Three on each side. You’ve drawn eight.”

Elias studied her face. “How would you know?”

“I crossed it yesterday.”

A milk cart rattled through the gate, erasing one of his chalk trees. Elias rose slowly.

“What is your name?”

“June.”

“June what?”

“Just June.”

She pointed beyond the gate. Silver grass bent beneath the wind.

“The road is there,” she said. “But it doesn’t like being remembered incorrectly.”

Then she walked into town.

Elias stood motionless until the chalk snapped between his fingers.

He found June an hour later in the market square, stealing an apple.

The fruit seller caught her wrist and shouted for the constable. Elias paid for the apple, though the seller insisted the girl had taken three others earlier. June denied this while chewing suspiciously quickly.

Elias led her to his workshop above the old printing house. Every wall was covered with maps. Some showed Bellweather as it had been a century ago, when the town was only a cluster of houses around a bell tower. Others showed coastlines, deserts, mountain passes, and islands shaped like sleeping animals.

In the center of the room stood a long table. Elias unrolled his final map of the Old East Road.

“Show me,” he said.

June wiped apple juice from her chin.

The map depicted the road in black ink, running from Bellweather through the villages of Orris, Saint Lume, and Farrowfield before reaching the eastern sea. The bridge lay seven miles from the town.

June leaned over it.

“This part is wrong,” she said, tapping the first curve. “There’s a well here.”

“There was never a well.”

“There is now.”

She traced the road with one dirty finger.

“This hill is gone. There’s a house here with yellow windows. The woman who lives there has no mouth, so don’t ask her questions.”

Elias stared at her.

June moved her finger farther east.

“Saint Lume is empty. The bell rings under the ground. Farrowfield is full of white birds, but they don’t fly. And the sea—”

She stopped.

“What about the sea?” Elias asked.

“I didn’t go that far.”

“Where did you come from?”

June looked toward the window.

Below, market voices rose and fell. A dog barked at a flock of geese. Ordinary sounds. Safe sounds.

“I came from the road,” she said.

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

Elias rolled up the map.

“Take me there.”

June shook her head at once.

“You said you crossed the road yesterday.”

“I did.”

“Then you can cross it again.”

“It won’t be the same road.”

“No road is ever exactly the same.”

“This one is.”

Her eyes were gray, Elias noticed, but not evenly so. Tiny flecks of green surrounded the pupils like fragments of a broken circle.

“It changes because people forget it,” she said. “Every forgotten thing has to become something else.”

Elias opened a cabinet and took out a leather map case, a compass, and a small brass measuring wheel. He had kept them clean for seventeen years.

“I haven’t forgotten,” he said.

June watched him gather his instruments.

“That might be worse.”

They left at noon.

At the eastern gate, June instructed Elias to close his eyes.

“That is not how cartography works,” he told her.

“It’s how this road works.”

Reluctantly, he obeyed.

“Now remember the sound of someone you miss,” she said.

Elias heard the wind in the silver grass. A wagon creaked behind them. From the gatehouse came a guard’s bored cough.

Then, beneath those sounds, he remembered Mara laughing.

She had laughed with her whole body, leaning forward and clutching his arm as though joy were a sudden storm. He remembered the night before her final journey. She had teased him for working too late and dropped a red ribbon across the unfinished map on his desk.

“You care more for roads than destinations,” she had said.

“And you care more for departures than returns,” he had replied.

He had meant it lightly. For seventeen years, those words had been stones in his chest.

“Open your eyes,” June whispered.

The silver field was gone.

A narrow road stretched beneath ash trees burning with red autumn leaves. Two ruts ran through the dark earth, filled with rainwater that reflected a cloudless sky. In the distance stood a stone well.

Elias could not breathe.

June stepped forward.

“Don’t look behind you,” she said.

He looked.

The eastern gate had disappeared. Behind them, the road continued into a dense wood.

“Now we have to go all the way,” June muttered.

Elias nearly laughed. The sound came out like a sob.

He fitted the measuring wheel to its handle and rolled it along the ground. The little counter clicked with each turn.

After half a mile, they reached the well. Elias inspected the stones, measured its width, and marked it in his notebook.

June waited with her arms crossed.

“What?” he asked.

“You think measuring it makes it stay?”

“That is generally the purpose.”

“No. Measuring only tells you how big it was while you were looking.”

Elias lowered a bucket into the well. It came back filled with seawater. A tiny silver fish leaped inside it.

He poured the water out.

They continued east.

By evening, the road curved toward a house with yellow windows. It stood alone in a bare field. Smoke rose from its chimney, though the air smelled not of woodsmoke but lavender.

“The woman with no mouth?” Elias asked.

June nodded. “We need to sleep somewhere.”

“I have a bedroll.”

“The dark is different here.”

Before he could ask how, the cottage door opened.

A tall woman in a blue dress beckoned them inside. Where her mouth should have been was only smooth skin.

The cottage contained three chairs, a table, and hundreds of clocks. They covered the walls from floor to ceiling. Some had hands that spun backward. Some ticked without moving. One chimed continuously in a small, frightened voice.

The woman served them soup.

Elias hesitated. June ate eagerly, so he tasted it. It was the same onion soup Mara used to make on winter evenings.

His spoon trembled.

The woman watched him. Her dark eyes were kind.

“You knew my wife,” he said.

June kicked his ankle under the table.

The mouthless woman tilted her head.

“Mara Vale,” Elias continued. “She traveled this road seventeen years ago. Did she come here?”

The clocks stopped.

Every one of them.

June seized Elias’s wrist.

The woman’s smooth face rippled. A line appeared where her lips should have been, widening into a black crack.

“Run,” June said.

They fled.

Behind them, the cottage windows went dark. The door slammed with enough force to shake the ground, and all the clocks began striking at once.

Night had fallen.

The darkness beyond the road was not empty. Shapes moved between the trees, tall as towers and thin as needles. They bent over the road but did not cross onto it.

Elias and June ran until the cottage’s terrible chiming faded.

At last they sheltered beneath an ash tree. June wrapped herself in her green coat. Elias spread his bedroll over both of them.

“You nearly got us killed,” she said.

“I asked a question.”

“You asked a forgotten thing to remember.”

“Is that why she had no mouth?”

June picked at a loose thread on her sleeve.

“She asked too many questions. The road answered.”

Elias opened his notebook. In the faint light of the moon, he sketched the cottage and wrote: Do not speak within.

“You still think you can map this place,” June said.

“I am mapping it.”

“Then draw those.”

She pointed toward the trees.

The towering shapes had gathered at the edge of the road. Though they had no visible faces, Elias felt their attention.

“What are they?”

“No one remembers.”

He closed the notebook.

In the morning, the cottage was gone. A field of yellow flowers had replaced it.

Elias said nothing.

They reached the River Orr near midday. The bridge had six posts, as June had said, but it crossed no water. Beneath its wooden planks lay a deep ravine filled with clouds.

Elias approached the edge. Far below, lightning flickered.

“The river is under the sky now,” June explained.

“That makes no sense.”

“It doesn’t have to.”

They crossed carefully.

On the other side stood the remains of Saint Lume. Roofless houses lined the road. Moss covered ovens and hearthstones. In the center of the village, a bell tolled beneath the earth.

At every note, the ruins changed.

A wall rose, then fell. A garden bloomed, withered, and became a graveyard. For an instant, villagers crowded the street: children chasing hoops, women carrying bread, an old man sleeping beneath a pear tree.

Then the bell sounded again, and all vanished.

Elias saw Mara beside a fountain.

She wore her red traveling cloak. Her hair was tied with the same ribbon she had left on his map.

“Mara!”

He ran toward her.

June caught his coat, but he pulled free.

Mara turned. Her face brightened.

“Elias?”

The buried bell tolled.

She disappeared. A burned doorway stood in her place.

Elias dropped to his knees.

The bell rang again, and Mara returned, closer now.

“You took so long,” she said.

He reached for her.

June struck him hard across the face.

The village vanished. They stood on an empty road, surrounded by gray mist.

Elias shoved June away.

“What have you done?”

“That wasn’t her.”

“She knew me.”

“The road knows you.”

He raised his hand, furious enough to strike her, but stopped.

June did not flinch. Her expression was older than any child’s should have been.

“It feeds you what you bring,” she said. “That’s why I told you it might be worse that you remembered.”

Elias lowered his hand.

The measuring wheel lay beside the road. Its counter, which had marked twelve miles, now read zero.

He sat in the dust.

“Then she is dead.”

“I didn’t say that.”

“You said the road invents what I hope to find.”

“No. I said it uses what you bring. Hope. Fear. Memory.” June looked into the mist. “Sometimes it uses the truth.”

The buried bell tolled again, far behind them.

“Why are you helping me?” Elias asked.

June was silent for a long time.

“Because I want to leave,” she said.

They continued toward Farrowfield.

The white birds were waiting.

Thousands stood in the fields on either side of the road. They resembled cranes, but each had four long legs and no wings. Their heads turned as Elias and June passed.

None made a sound.

At the abandoned Farrowfield inn, they found food laid on a table: warm bread, cheese, pears, and two cups of tea.

Elias touched the teapot. It was hot.

“Someone is here,” he said.

June had gone pale.

At the far end of the room hung a mirror.

In it, Elias saw himself standing alone.

He turned toward June. She was beside him. In the mirror, she did not exist.

“Who are you?” he asked.

June backed away.

“Who are you?”

“I told you.”

“You told me a name.”

Outside, the white birds began stamping their feet. The sound rolled across the fields like rain.

June reached into her coat and took out a faded red ribbon.

Elias recognized the dark stain at one end, where he had once spilled ink.

He gripped the edge of the table.

“Where did you get that?”

“She gave it to me.”

“Mara?”

June nodded.

“She found me on the road. I don’t know how long ago. Time doesn’t stay in order here.”

“Where is she?”

“At the sea.”

“Alive?”

June’s eyes filled with tears.

“I don’t know what that means anymore.”

The walls of the inn shuddered. In the mirror, Elias’s reflection turned its head, though he had not moved.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because she said you would come if I took the ribbon, and if you came, one of us could leave.”

“One of us?”

“The road only gives back what it takes if something else stays.”

The mirror cracked.

A hand pressed against the other side of the glass.

June grabbed Elias’s map case.

“We have to go.”

They ran from the inn as the mirror burst behind them.

The white birds stamped faster. One by one, they lowered their bodies and leaped into the air. Their four legs stretched outward like pale branches. Though wingless, they rose above the fields and circled the darkening sky.

Elias and June followed the road east.

By dusk, they smelled salt.

The sea appeared suddenly beyond a line of black dunes. It was perfectly still, its surface smooth as metal. No waves touched the shore.

A woman stood at the water’s edge.

Her red cloak moved in a wind Elias could not feel.

He stopped.

Seventeen years had changed him. His hair had gone gray. His back had bent. Lines had settled around his eyes and mouth.

Mara looked exactly as she had on the morning of her departure.

June remained behind on the dunes.

Elias walked to his wife.

Mara smiled.

This time, she did not vanish.

He touched her face. Her skin was warm.

“I am sorry,” he whispered.

“For what?”

“For telling you that you never returned.”

Mara placed her hand over his.

“But I didn’t.”

He began to laugh, and then they were holding each other. He buried his face in her hair. She smelled of rain, ink, and woodsmoke.

For one impossible minute, seventeen years collapsed.

Then Mara stepped back.

“You cannot stay,” she said.

“I came to take you home.”

“There is no home for me now.”

“Bellweather is still there.”

“For you. Not for me.”

He showed her his notebook, his instruments, the map case hanging at his side.

“I can map a way back.”

Mara’s expression softened.

“You always believed a line on paper could make the world behave.”

“A good map can.”

“No,” she said. “A good map helps people accept that the world will not.”

Behind them, June sat on the dunes, hugging her knees.

Mara looked toward her.

“I found her wandering near Saint Lume,” she said. “She remembered nothing. Not her parents, not her village, not even her name.”

“Then why June?”

“It was the month I found her.”

Elias studied the girl. “Why doesn’t she appear in mirrors?”

“Because the road has nearly forgotten her.”

The still sea darkened as night approached.

Mara took the ribbon from June and pressed it into Elias’s hand.

“The road requires an exchange,” she said. “One lost traveler for another.”

“Then I will stay. You and June can go.”

Mara shook her head. “Only one.”

“You go.”

“I have been here too long. If I returned, the years would return with me.”

“I don’t care.”

“I do.”

Her voice broke.

Elias understood then. She was not waiting to be rescued. She had brought him there to say farewell—and to save the child.

He wanted to argue. He wanted to tear up his maps and curse every road he had ever drawn. Instead, he held Mara’s ribbon and listened to the silence of the sea.

“What happens to you?” he asked.

“I become part of the road.”

“Is that death?”

“Perhaps. But I have spent seventeen years learning that a name matters less than we think.”

“It matters to me.”

“I know.”

She kissed him.

The sea moved.

A single wave reached the shore, black beneath the moon. When it withdrew, Mara’s footprints were gone.

So was she.

Elias stood alone until June took his hand.

The return journey lasted one night and seventeen years.

They passed through Farrowfield, where the white birds had become marble statues. They crossed the bridge, beneath which the River Orr flowed in its proper place. They came to Saint Lume and found it whole, though everyone there was asleep and could not be awakened.

At dawn, the eastern gate appeared ahead.

June stopped.

“What if it doesn’t let me through?”

Elias took the red ribbon and tied it around her wrist.

“Then we will stay together.”

They crossed beneath the arch.

Bellweather was waking. Bakers opened shutters. Chimneys smoked. A milk cart rattled over the stones.

Behind them lay only silver grass.

The gatekeeper stared at Elias.

“Master Vale? You’ve been gone three days.”

Elias looked at June. She was reflected in the window of the gatehouse.

He began to weep.

Years later, travelers spoke of the maps made by Elias Vale and his daughter, June. Their charts were unusual. In the empty spaces beyond familiar roads, they did not draw monsters or write warnings.

Instead, they left those regions blank.

June grew into a cartographer as skilled as her father, though she preferred mapping paths through forests and mountains to charting towns. She claimed roads were more honest where no one had named them.

Elias never again drew the Old East Road beneath the gate.

He made only one final map of it.

The map showed no distances. It offered no scale and marked no villages. A single pale line ran eastward across the page, crossing a river, passing through a field of white birds, and ending at a black sea.

At the shore, Elias drew a woman in a red cloak.

Then, with the smallest stroke of his pen, he continued the road across the water.
